newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania to privatise three state banks by 2000.
newsitem.headline: Albania to privatise three state banks by 2000.

text.p: Albania's government hopes to complete the privatisation of three state banks by the year 2000, a government official said on Tuesday.

Albert Gajo, economic adviser to Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi, told Reuters the government would begin privatisation proceedings for Rural Commercial Bank (RCB), National Commercial Bank (NCB) and Savings Bank very soon.
"The government committed itself to concluding the privatisation of the three commercial second-level state banks by 2000," he said.
Gajo said Rural Commercial Bank would be the first to be privatised as it needed no restructuring and had begun with no capital.
"By the beginning of next year its privatisation procedures will start," he said. "The two other banks need about two years of restructuring," Gajo added.

The banks would be privatised by selling shares to foreign and local investors and the general public, the government said. But it noted no individual or company would be allowed to buy more than a 10 percent stake in any of the banks, unless the company itself held a licence as a bank.
"That (provision) was made to ensure the buyers would still keep the banks functioning in the country," Gajo said.
The IMF and World Bank are supervising Albania's bank privatisation strategy.
"They began a privatisation program two years ago but now that our government has committed itself formally, they will play a much greater role (in the privatisation)," Gajo said.
Gajo said the state would continue to retain majority control in the first three to four years of privatisation.
"The aim is to end the government's majority control, but in the first three to four years of privatisation, financial stability should be preserved," he said.
"Even if 100 percent is sold some conditions for operating will need to be defined," he added.
Albania set up a two-tier bank system with the Bank of Albania serving as the central institution to the National Commercial Bank, the Rural Commercial Bank and the Savings Bank.
The National Commercial Bank is the shareholder of two joint venture banks, the Albanian-Italian Bank with Italy's Banca di Roma, and the Arab-Albanian Islamic Bank.
Albania's central bank has given licences to two Greek banks and a Malaysian investor to set up private banks in the Balkan state.
